newsitem.title: RUSSIA: RUSSIA'S YELTSIN ANNOUNCES REFORM OF THE ROUBLE.
newsitem.headline: RUSSIA'S YELTSIN ANNOUNCES REFORM OF THE ROUBLE.

text.p: Russia will knock three zeroes off its bloated rouble from the start of next year now that the hyper-inflationary price rises of recent years are history, President Boris Yeltsin said on Monday.
"Today we have taken a decision which affects all of us," Yeltsin said in an address to the nation. "From January 1, 1998, Russia will carry out a thousandfold redenomination of the rouble."
"From January 1, 1998, we will pay one rouble for goods costing 1,000 roubles."

Yeltsin said though the redenomination would take place at the beginning of next year, current notes would be usable until the end of 1998. After that Russians would have another four years to exchange old roubles for new.

The currency redenomination, crowning several years of tough economic reforms, will make life easier for everyone from oil companies to old age pensioners who now have to wrestle with millions, billions and even trillions of roubles in transactions.

The value of the rouble has plunged since the Soviet Union broke up in 1991. It was artificially pegged at 0.55 to the U.S. dollar during the Soviet era, spawning a huge foreign exchange black market.
On Monday, the rouble was less than one fiftieth of one U.S. cent on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange.

Inflation rose to over one thousand percent on an annualised basis in late 1993, but has slowed steadily to 15 percent in June this year, and the central bank has been holding the rouble relatively steady since the middle of 1995.
Price stability had allowed the redenomination to take place, Yeltsin said in his address.

"The prices of basic goods are practically stable and we are determined and certain that they will remain so. That is why we took this decision to carry out a monetary reform. And with it we declare today: There will be no more inflation," he said.
Yeltsin took pains to assure Russians that they would not lose out as a result of the currency reform. Painful experience from the recent past will be fresh in Russians' memories.
In the last currency reform debacle they were forced to exchange old high-denomination rouble notes for new ones in 1991, but were given only three days to do so.
The result of the drastic deflationary step was a wave of panic, huge queues outside banks, and millions of people with savings wiped out overnight.
"Nobody will lose anything as a result of this reform," Yeltsin said, adding that people would not be forced to swap their banknotes for new ones.
The latest currency reform is being viewed both in practical and psychological terms.
For one, financial transactions would be made much simpler.
"The redenomination of the rouble...will definitely make life easier for people. Without superfluous zeroes it will be easier and more normal to carry out transactions."
But it was also aimed at restoring confidence in the rouble, encouraging Russians to hold their accounts in the national currency rather than rushing to the safe haven of the dollar or the mark.
"Once you receive your wages, it is no longer necessary today as it was not long ago to run to the exchange kiosk. You can keep your bank savings in rouble accounts," he said.
Yeltsin also assured Russians that the inflationary measure of printing banknotes to generate cash would not be repeated.
"People must know for sure that we will not try to solve the country's economic problems with the help of the printing press," he said.
